# Independent audit: inverse-power depth and effective cap count

Auditor: `minkowski_transfer`. Verdict: **PASS** for
`candidate 55fd8fec61360536`, all sections and
all stated quantifiers. This audit uses the independently checked radial
and projective dependency recorded in
`historical context (not an accepted premise)`.
No numerical test is needed for this continuous and finite-cover proof.

## 1. The maximum is attained at an actual interior point

The cap function G(y,u) is jointly continuous for arbitrary finite
(y,u), with u on the unit sphere: away from the limiting hyperplane,
its indicators converge pointwise, and integrable f dominates them.
A hyperplane is f-null because f is a density. Minimization over the
compact sphere consequently gives continuous D_f. This minimum also
represents the infimum over all closed containing halfspaces, since
moving a boundary to pass through y can only decrease its cap mass.

At infinity the particular through-y cap with normal y/|y| lies outside
the radius-|y| ball, so the depth tends to zero. At an interior support
point a small ball has a uniform positive lower density bound, because
phi is continuous and bounded above there. Each through-center cap
captures half of that ball. Thus a positive maximum exists on a large
compact ball. A point outside the open convex support has a separating
or supporting containing halfspace with zero mass. The maximizing point
therefore belongs to the actual open support U, not merely its closure.

## 2. Active normals and the ordinary radial-body transfer

The active-normal set is nonempty and compact. If its convex hull
missed zero, strict separation would give one direction v with a
uniform strictly positive scalar product against all active normals.
This remains positive on an open neighborhood of the active set.
Moving y a small distance in the negative v direction expands all
these caps. A fixed small ball about y supplies a uniform slab-volume
lower bound proportional to the movement, and f has a uniform positive
lower bound on that ball. Thus their masses uniformly increase. On
the compact complement, the original strict gap above the minimum
persists by uniform continuity. This contradicts maximality. No
unsupported differentiability of f or of the maximizing normal is used.

Caratheodory yields finitely many active unit normals with positive
weights and zero sum, after dropping zero weights. Their closed
through-y caps cover the whole ambient space: a point missed by all
would have strictly negative weighted scalar product, contradicting
zero balance. The audited inverse-power radial construction preserves
all these cap masses and the total mass in an actual r-dimensional
convex body. Its ordinary centroid lies in at least one selected cap,
which has mass Q. Ordinary Gruenbaum therefore gives exactly
`Q>=gamma_r M`. The selected point for the original density remains
the previously attained y in U; it is not replaced by this auxiliary
body's centroid.

For a closed convex restriction L of positive f-mass, L has nonempty
interior and U intersect int(L) is nonempty. Otherwise its intersection
with U would lie on the Lebesgue-null boundary of a full-dimensional
convex set. Restricting phi to that open convex intersection retains
its inverse-power hypothesis; the discarded boundary has zero mass.
Thus the depth guarantee is genuinely hereditary under every stated
positive-mass convex restriction. The argument includes r=1.

## 3. Distal truncation for all alpha>=0

For every cap with A_i>alpha, a parallel distal cap of mass A_i-alpha
exists by continuous cap tails. At alpha=0 its original threshold
itself is available, even if its mass is the total mass; the resulting
inequality is also simply the union bound. For alpha>0 every requested
nontrivial tail level is strictly below total mass. Unbounded support
causes no problem because finite mass gives zero limiting tail at
positive infinity and full mass at negative infinity.

Intersecting the retained closed sides gives a closed convex restriction.
The hyperplanes separating removed and retained sides have zero f-mass,
so either choice of boundary ownership gives the same exact mass laws.
The remainder mass is at least `M-sum(A_i-alpha)_+`, and each original
cap has remainder mass at most alpha. If this lower bound is positive,
the hereditary depth point in the remainder belongs to an original cap
because the original caps cover the support. This gives
`gamma_r M_remainder<=alpha`. If the lower bound is nonpositive, the
claimed positive-part inequality is immediate. Empty caps, untrimmed
caps with mass at most alpha, and full caps are all included.

## 4. General projective exponent and preserved masses

There are r projective v coordinates, one t coordinate, and D-r-1
remaining y coordinates. The first substitution v=tz contributes t^r.
Then t=1/s contributes s^-2 and y=w/s contributes s^(-(D-r-1)).
The total factor is exactly s^(-(D+1)), independently of r.
The perspective domain is convex by the same positive-s-weighted
mixture checked in the three-cap audit. Its density to power
-1/(D+1) is the affine coordinate s. There are D-r integrated
variables, so functional BBL gives exactly

    [-1/(D+1)]/[1-(D-r)/(D+1)]=-1/(r+1).

Its parameter condition is satisfied strictly. This invokes only the
ordinary functional BBL statement independently checked in Bobkov's
Lemma 2.3 in the preceding audit, with no symmetry assumption.

The original compact body bounds t and y, giving a uniform finite
bound for the displayed marginal density. Its positive interior is
full-dimensional and convex. Passing to this open support representative
changes only a Lebesgue-null boundary. The original t=0 set also has
zero volume because t is nonconstant. Every original cap involved in
the coordinate construction depends only on (v,t), so its mass is
preserved by the actual real change of integration variables. The
fixed positive affine Jacobian affects neither normalized masses nor
inverse-power convexity.

## 5. Minimal subcovers and the effective dimension

An inclusion-minimal subcover exists because the original family is
finite. A one-cap subcover has mass V; then
`(V-alpha)_++alpha/gamma_s>=V` directly for every alpha>=0. This also
handles m=1 and s=0 without applying any zero-dimensional density
argument or undefined exponent convention.

For j>=2, the normal rank rho is at least one and at most j. If
rho<=j-1, orthogonal projection to the normal span preserves every
cap mass, with a log-concave density on its positive interior. The
hereditary theorem and truncation apply in dimension rho. The exact
comparison is

    rho<=min(D,j-1)<=min(D,m-1)=s,
    gamma_rho>=gamma_s.

Therefore enlarging the nonnegative alpha coefficient from
1/gamma_rho to 1/gamma_s is in the required direction. Restoring the
omitted nonnegative positive-part summands preserves the inequality.

If rho=j, then j<=D and the affine margin map is onto R^j. Its compact
full-dimensional image misses the open negative orthant. Separation
gives nonnegative coefficients and a nonnegative weighted margin on K.
If any coefficient vanished, the positive-coefficient caps would be a
proper subcover, contrary to minimality. All coefficients are positive,
and their weighted margin t is nonconstant by linear independence.
It is positive throughout int(K). The stated affine coordinates exist
because the margins have rank j.

The projective images have weighted margin sum one, hence cover all
of R^(j-1). They are genuine halfspaces: if one projected normal
vanished, its original margin would be proportional to t, yielding
a linear relation among the j independent margins because j>=2 and
all separator coefficients are positive. The general marginal formula
now gives inverse-power exponent -1/j in dimension j-1. Applying the
hereditary theorem and truncation gives gamma_(j-1), and
`j-1<=s` again permits the claimed coefficient enlargement. This
exhausts every possible rank without assuming j<=D+1 in advance.

Taking alpha equal to the minimum of all m original masses yields
exactly the displayed minimum-overlap inequality, including a zero
minimum. No omitted cap enters this algebra with a negative summand.

## 6. Sharpness and exact scope

For m-1<=D and m>=2, the product of an (m-1)-simplex with any body
in the remaining dimensions has m canonical centroid caps, all of mass
`gamma_(m-1)V`. They cover the body. Testing alpha at that common
mass makes all positive-part terms zero, so any larger proposed depth
factor fails. In remaining dimension zero, the product factor is the
single zero-dimensional point with measure one.

For m-1>D, the D+1 canonical caps and additional empty caps also make
all positive-part terms zero at alpha=gamma_D V. This correctly proves
sharpness of the positive-part factor gamma_D despite the added caps
having zero mass. That example does not itself certify sharpness of
the derived minimum-overlap coefficient because its minimum is zero;
the source only asserts sharpness of the factor. If desired, repeating
canonical caps instead makes all m masses equal and makes both formulas
an equality. For m=1, the single full cap proves gamma_0=1 directly.

The final fiberwise scope is accurate: upon restriction to an affine
fiber, whole and empty traces can be handled separately, while genuine
cuts fall under the ordinary-dimensional theorem. No common choice of
fiber cap ordering, trimming thresholds, or mixed-integer center has
been supplied or asserted. The theorem provides ordinary cap-budget
inequalities with their exact effective dimension; it does not complete
the mixed arithmetic combination step.

No correction is required.
